title: Competitor Distance Map: Store Spacing Measured
description: Plot your location against competitors and read the straight-line separation with the Competitor Distance Map — spacing for market decisions. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, two Midtown Manhattan locations — Times Square and Grand Central — sit approx. 0.9 km (0.6 miles) apart: in dense retail, that gap can be a whole market; in a suburb it would be nothing.
quick_answer: The Competitor Distance Map plots your business location against competitor locations and measures the straight-line separation and bearing between them. It answers the spacing questions behind site decisions — how close is the nearest rival, and where is the gap — with geography instead of impressions.

When a franchisee claims a new rival store breaches an agreed spacing, this map produces the number the agreement is actually about — straight-line separation between the two doors.
A rival opening nearby is a distance fact before it is a panic: measure it. Half a mile in a city centre and five miles in a rural market are different events wearing the same headline.
Chains auditing their own estate use pairwise spacing to spot the two stores quietly splitting one catchment — the map shows the overlap a spreadsheet of addresses hides.

Times Square (40.7580, −73.9855) to Grand Central (40.7527, −73.9772): approx. 0.9 km (0.6 mi), bearing 130°. Two locations can be this close and serve different flows entirely — the number frames the question; footfall answers it.

From downtown Chicago, the same-brand question looks different: Oak Park is approx. 8.0 miles (12.8 km) out and Evanston 11.7 miles (18.8 km). At suburban scale, gaps of this size are separate markets — the map keeps the two scales from being judged by one rule.

popular_table.title: Reading separation distances
popular_table.intro: There is no universal 'too close' — but separation bands mean different things in different retail geographies. These are reading conventions for the numbers this tool returns, not rules.
popular_table.note: Straight-line separation ignores road access and barriers; two stores 1 mile apart across a river with one bridge can be further apart in practice than two stores 3 miles apart on one road.

faq: Straight-line or driving distance — which matters for spacing?

Agreements and territory rules are almost always written on straight-line separation, which is what this map measures. Customer behaviour follows roads, so use driving tools for the demand side of the same decision.
Can I plot more than one competitor?
Yes — add each rival location and read its separation from yours. The pattern of gaps matters more than any single pair.
Does it show who is winning?
No. It measures geography only: no sales, footfall or review data. Distance frames the competition; it does not score it.
What if the competitor is inside a mall or upstairs?
Use the building's coordinates; at market scale the vertical and indoor detail is below the precision the spacing question needs.
Can I measure my own two stores?
Yes — the geometry is identical, and chains use it for cannibalisation reviews exactly as franchise teams use it for territory checks.
Which point of a large store counts?
Use a consistent convention — main entrance or site centroid — and keep it across all locations, or the comparisons drift by more than the decision tolerates.
Locations are plotted in your browser session; nothing about your estate is published by measuring it.
